meta.notes: Story-mode steps; bodies are templated at export time from the exported numbers. Each selector starts with the data-story attribute the screen renders (story_id), optionally narrowed to a child element so the step card does not cover its subject: aog-incident-ps1, aircraft, rotable-float-calc, network-bom, action-inbox, frontier-chart. mobile_selector (or null) is the narrower target used at <= 480 px (bottom-sheet layout); it also starts with the story_id hook. title_simple / body_simple are the Simple-mode (plain English) text, computed from the same numbers; title / body are the Expert text.

steps.title: 1 · The operational problem
steps.body: A6-FHW (fictional) is on the ground at BOM: a D0 nose wheel steering actuator (NB) failed and none was held there. The part reached it after 9 h; with fitting, it was released at 14 h. Ranked on what the desk knew then, the best route was: Transfer from AUH.
steps.body_simple: A plane is stuck at Mumbai. A part it needs before its next flight broke, and no spare was kept there. The part arrived after 9 hours, and the plane flew again after 14 hours.

steps.title: 2 · Diagnose the shortage
steps.body: ATA 32 rates URGENT, led by GN-32-R014, a D0 nose wheel steering actuator (NB) with risk 100/100. With 0 units at BOM under the Simple Rulebook, it caused 464 AOG h across all stations in the last 52 weeks (W52–W103) of this simulation.
steps.body_simple: The landing gear group is the biggest risk, and one part leads it. With no spare at Mumbai, it kept planes grounded for 464 hours across all airports in the last year.

steps.title: 3 · The repair pipeline
steps.body: Pooled over the 72-day repair loop, the Network Plan's 17 spares cover over 99.9% of removals. At BOM the question is resupply: the Network Plan holds 2 units there (Simple Rulebook: 0), refilled from AUH in about 4.3 days, so 99.7% of D0 needs find a unit on the shelf.
steps.body_simple: Broken parts go away for repair for about 72 days. To always have one ready, the airline needs enough spares to cover the ones away in repair. The Network Plan keeps 17 in total, so a spare is almost always on the shelf. At Mumbai it keeps 2, refilled from Abu Dhabi in about 4 days.

steps.title: 4 · Compare the trade-offs
steps.body: In this simulation, across 120 modelled part numbers: at BOM, holdout material AOG falls from 242 h/yr under the Simple Rulebook to 6 under the Network Plan (11 rotables here). Network Plan + Extra Spares adds 1 more here and takes network AOG to 76 h/yr. Each emergency hop from AUH takes 9 h.
steps.body_simple: In this simulation, at Mumbai, the Simple Rulebook left planes grounded 242 hours a year. The Network Plan cuts that to 6 hours. Across all 120 modelled part numbers, the Network Plan + Extra Spares brings the network total down to 76 hours a year.

steps.title: 5 · Recommend the action
steps.body: The action centre raises 63 exceptions for W103, 25 urgent. At BOM, GN-32-R014 has 0 of 2 on hand, with 7 D0 requests and 75 AOG h there in the last 52 weeks (W52–W103). Action: Position 2 units at BOM (station target 0 -> 2); AUH has none serviceable — source via repair/exchange.
steps.body_simple: The planner's list has 63 alerts this week, 25 of them urgent. Mumbai has 0 of the 2 spares it should hold for this part. The advice is to send 2 there.

steps.title: 6 · Business value on the Readiness Frontier
steps.body: In this simulation, across 120 modelled part numbers, the Network Plan cuts material AOG by 1,480 h a year vs the Simple Rulebook. It buys 68 rotables (≈AED 8.4M) and removes 20 (≈AED 3.1M); average simulated inventory +AED 0.6M. Network Plan + Extra Spares adds AED 7.6M for 134 h/yr less [87–181].
steps.body_simple: In this simulation, across 120 modelled part numbers, the Network Plan cuts grounded time by 1,480 hours a year. It buys 68 repairable spares (about AED 8.4M) and removes 20 (about AED 3.1M). Average stock value rises by about AED 0.6M. Spending AED 7.6M more saves about 134 hours more.
